---
title: "Donor recruitment and screening"
order: 2
---

## The ticket

Marcus Webb shows up at a Lakeshore Blood Center mobile drive parked outside a downtown
office tower on a Monday. He registers, answers the Donor History Questionnaire (DHQ — the
standardized medical history interview every donor completes before donating), and moves to
vitals. His hemoglobin comes back under the cutoff. The phlebotomist defers him on the spot:
temporary deferral, come back once his levels are back in range, no needle today.

Thursday, three days later, Marcus shows up at a different Lakeshore drive — a grocery store
parking lot across town — and registers again. Same person, same eligibility problem, but a
different site, different staff, and (he hopes) a clean slate.

This is the moment donor recruitment and screening exists to catch. Not "will this donor lie" —
most don't. It's "does Lakeshore's system actually know, at *this* site, on *this* day, that
this donor was turned away three days ago at a site forty minutes away?" If the answer is no,
everything downstream — the draw, the testing, the label, the transfusion — inherits a decision
that was never actually made correctly. That's the gap this module closes: recruitment, drive
logistics, registration, the DHQ, the eligibility criteria, the deferral decision, and the
record that has to prove all of it happened before anyone reaches for a needle.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

The failure mode is blunt: if a donor who shouldn't donate — because of a health risk to
themselves, or a risk their blood poses to a recipient — donates anyway, that unit exists and
has to be tracked down and stopped before it reaches a patient. Everything after collection
(testing, quarantine, component separation, labeling, release) is built on the assumption that
the donor was actually eligible on the day of the draw. Get eligibility wrong and every later
control is compensating for a mistake that should never have entered the pipeline.

You already run a version of this problem, just with a different noun. Think of donor
eligibility screening as **an intake gate with a documented decision** — the same shape as a
service request that can't proceed to fulfillment until intake criteria are checked and the
decision is logged, not waved through because the requester seems trustworthy. Nobody skips
the intake gate because "the requester probably qualifies."

The sharper bridge is what actually failed in the Marcus Webb scenario, or nearly did: **donor
identity and the deferral registry are authoritative master data, and this data has to be a
single source of truth consulted before service is delivered.** You know exactly what happens
when a CMDB has two records for the same configuration item because a hostname got entered two
different ways — nobody notices until the two records disagree about something that matters,
usually during an incident. A donor record works the same way, except the "incident" is a
donor with a documented health risk being drawn anyway because the system didn't recognize him
as the same person it deferred on Monday. A stale or unmerged donor record isn't a housekeeping
annoyance here — it's a data-quality defect with a patient-safety consequence, and it's exactly
as preventable as a duplicate CI record, for the same reason: consistent identity capture at the
point of intake.

## The rule, in plain English

Before Lakeshore can collect a single unit of blood from anyone, on any given day, four things
have to happen, in this order:

1. **Check the deferral registry first.** Before anything else, the donor's identity has to be
   checked against the record of everyone currently deferred or ineligible — not asked, checked.
2. **Confirm identity and the donation interval.** Who is this person, provably, and has enough
   time passed since their last donation.
3. **Take the medical history.** The DHQ interview, covering specific risk factors the
   regulation names — not a generic "do you feel healthy" conversation.
4. **Perform the physical assessment.** Temperature, blood pressure, hemoglobin/hematocrit,
   pulse, weight, a skin check — objective vitals against fixed numeric limits, not judgment
   calls.

If any of the four turns up a problem, the donor is deferred, not drawn — and Lakeshore has a
separate, time-bound obligation to tell the donor why. Marcus's hemoglobin failure on Monday
should have produced two things: a deferral entered into the registry that Thursday's site can
actually see, and a notification to Marcus about what happened and why. The scenario only works
as a near-miss if the first of those two things is where the process is thin.

The system that holds all of this — the deferral registry, the day's eligibility
determinations, the record that a decision was made — is Lakeshore's Blood Establishment
Computer Software (BECS): the system of record for donor eligibility and deferrals. That's all
you need to know about BECS for this module; what makes it different from an ordinary
enterprise application is the whole subject of module 5, later in this course.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 630.10(d)(1) | "Six-thirty point one-oh, paragraph d, sub-one" | Before collection, the establishment must consult the records of deferred donors maintained under 606.160(e). | The exact check that Thursday's drive site has to run on Marcus before he reaches vitals — not after. |
| 21 CFR 630.10(e) | "Six-thirty point one-oh, paragraph e" | The medical history interview (the DHQ) must assess named risk-factor categories before collection. | The Monday interview that first surfaced whatever put Marcus's eligibility in question that day. |
| 21 CFR 630.10(f)(3) | "Six-thirty point one-oh, paragraph f, sub-three" | Hemoglobin or hematocrit must meet fixed numeric minimums; below them, the donor doesn't donate. | The specific, numeric reason Monday's phlebotomist deferred Marcus — not a judgment call. |
| 21 CFR 630.10(g)(1) | "Six-thirty point one-oh, paragraph g, sub-one" | The establishment must obtain proof of identity from the donor, not just a name. | What Thursday's registration clerk needs to actually match Marcus against Monday's deferral — a self-reported name isn't enough. |
| 21 CFR 630.10(h) | "Six-thirty point one-oh, paragraph h" | An establishment must not collect from a donor found ineligible, must defer them, and must notify them under 630.40. | The rule Thursday's site would violate if Marcus were drawn anyway. |
| 21 CFR 630.40(a) and (c) | "Six-thirty point four-oh, paragraphs a and c" | Deferred or ineligible donors must be notified of the deferral and its reason, with reasonable attempts made within 8 weeks, documented either way. | Lakeshore's separate obligation to Marcus, running in parallel to the registry check, regardless of whether Thursday catches him. |

## The actual text

Start with the check that has to happen before anything else, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/630.10.md` (retrieved from eCFR):

> (d) *How must you determine the eligibility of a donor?* You must determine the donor's
> eligibility before collection of blood or blood components, by the following procedures:
>
> (1) You must consult the records of deferred donors maintained under § 606.160(e)(1) and (2)
> of this chapter. Exception: If pre-collection review of the record described in
> § 606.160(e)(2) of this chapter is not feasible because you cannot consult the cumulative
> record at the collection site, you must consult the cumulative record prior to release of any
> blood or blood component prepared from the collection.

Read that exception carefully — it doesn't excuse skipping the check, it moves the deadline.
If a mobile drive site genuinely cannot reach the cumulative record live (a real operational
constraint for a site with intermittent connectivity), Lakeshore still has to consult it before
the unit is *released*, not before the draw. That's a narrower safety net than it sounds: the
donor already got drawn by the time this exception applies. It is not a license to skip the
check at intake.

The medical history requirement that produced Marcus's deferral candidate list in the first
place:

> (e) *How do you assess the donor's medical history?* Before collection you must conduct a
> medical history interview as described in this section to determine if the donor is in good
> health; to identify risk factors closely associated with exposure to, or clinical evidence of
> a relevant transfusion-transmitted infection; and to determine if there are other conditions
> that may adversely affect the health of the donor or the safety, purity, or potency of the
> blood or blood components or any product manufactured from the blood or blood components.

And the specific, numeric criterion that actually deferred him — not a subjective judgment,
a hard number:

> (3) *Hemoglobin or hematocrit determination.* You must determine the donor's hemoglobin level
> or hematocrit value by using a sample of blood obtained by fingerstick, venipuncture, or by a
> method that provides equivalent results. Blood obtained from the earlobe is not acceptable.

(The section goes on to set the actual thresholds — 12.5 g/dL or 38% hematocrit minimum for
female allogeneic donors, 13.0 g/dL or 39% for male allogeneic donors, with a narrower
alternative standard available for female donors under a specific FDA-accepted procedure. The
number matters less here than the shape of the rule: it's fixed, it's measured, and it isn't
negotiable at the point of vitals.)

The identity requirement that Thursday's registration clerk actually needs to lean on:

> (g) *Are there additional requirements for determining the eligibility of the donor?* You must
> obtain the following from the donor on the day of donation:
>
> (1) *Proof of identity and postal address.* You must obtain proof of identity of the donor and
> a postal address where the donor may be contacted for 8 weeks after donation.

And the consequence, if any of the above turns up a problem:

> (h) *What must you do when a donor is not eligible?* You must not collect blood or blood
> components from a donor found to be ineligible prior to collection based on criteria in
> §§ 630.10 or 630.15, or deferred under § 610.41 of this chapter or § 630.30(b)(2), unless this
> subchapter provides an exception. You must defer donors found to be ineligible and you must
> notify the donor of their deferral under § 630.40.

That last sentence hands off to a separate regulation — 630.40 — which is worth its own look,
because it's a "must," not a "should," and it runs on its own clock, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/630.40.md`:

> (a) *Notification of donors.* You, an establishment that collects blood or blood components,
> must make reasonable attempts to notify any donor... who has been determined not to be
> eligible as a donor based on eligibility criteria under §§ 630.10 and 630.15.
>
> (c) *Time period for notification.* You must make reasonable attempts to notify the donor
> within 8 weeks after determining that the donor is deferred or determined not to be eligible
> for donation as described in paragraph (a) of this section. You must document that you have
> successfully notified the donor or when you are unsuccessful that you have made reasonable
> attempts to notify the donor.

Notice what 630.40 doesn't say: it doesn't say "notify the donor so they don't come back." It
requires notification and documentation of the attempt, full stop — a separate obligation to
Marcus that exists whether or not Thursday's site catches him. Both things have to work: the
registry check that stops the second draw, and the notification that Lakeshore owed Marcus
regardless.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator reconstructing this scenario doesn't ask Lakeshore to describe its process.
They ask for three specific artifacts, and a gap in any one is a finding on its own:

**The donor record from Monday**, showing the DHQ responses, the vitals, the specific
hemoglobin value that triggered the deferral, and who made the determination. This is what
630.10(e) and (f) require to exist — not "the donor was deferred," but the actual basis for the
decision, in enough detail to reconstruct it.

**The cumulative deferred-donor record** — the registry itself — showing Marcus entered on
Monday's date, with a timestamp that predates Thursday's registration attempt. This is what
630.10(d)(1) requires be consulted, maintained under 606.160(e), which already sits in
`sources/cfr/606.160.md`: "Establishments must maintain at each location a record of all donors
found to be ineligible or deferred at that location so that blood and blood components from an
ineligible donor are not collected and/or released while the donor is ineligible or deferred."
In practice at Lakeshore, this registry lives inside BECS — that's the whole reason BECS is
named in this module: it's the system an inspector expects to see actually queried, with a
timestamp, at Thursday's site.

**The notification record** — proof that Lakeshore attempted to tell Marcus about the Monday
deferral within 8 weeks, per 630.40(c), and documented either the successful contact or the
failed attempts. Ownership here typically sits with donor services or the Quality Analyst who
audits deferral notification compliance, not with the phlebotomist who ran Monday's interview.

A bad answer to "how do you know a deferred donor can't donate at a different site" sounds like
"our staff would recognize a repeat donor" or "he'd have to lie on the DHQ to get through." Both
describe a hope, not a control. The control an inspector is looking for is a system query against
a shared registry, timestamped, at the point of registration — before vitals, before the DHQ,
before anyone reaches for a needle.

## Common traps

**"The DHQ is just paperwork the donor fills out before the real screening starts."** It isn't
paperwork adjacent to the eligibility determination — under 630.10(e), it *is* the eligibility
determination, or at least the largest part of it. A DHQ response entered wrong, skipped, or
rushed through isn't a data-entry inconvenience; it's the regulatory basis for the day's
decision failing to get made. Treat a sloppy DHQ process with the same seriousness you'd treat a
change record approved without anyone actually reading the change.

**"A donor's ID card, or the name they give at registration, is close enough to check the
registry."** This is exactly where the Marcus Webb scenario nearly breaks. 630.10(g)(1) requires
*proof* of identity — not a self-reported name, not a donor's own assurance that they weren't
deferred. If Thursday's site matches Marcus against the deferral registry using only the name he
gives verbally, and he goes by a middle name, or the Monday site logged an address typo, the
match can silently fail — not because anyone lied, but because the identity data wasn't captured
consistently enough to resolve as the same person. That's the master-data problem from the ITSM
bridge above, showing up as a live control gap, not a hypothetical one.

## What this means for your job

- **Don't accept "the donor would have been recognized" as an answer to how the deferral
  registry works.** Ask specifically what identity fields the registration process captures, and
  whether those fields are enough to resolve two records as the same person across sites — a
  name-only match is not a control, it's a coincidence that usually works.
- **Ask your Quality Analyst how BECS timestamps a deferral versus when a different site's
  registration can actually see it.** A deferral entered Monday afternoon that isn't visible
  system-wide until an overnight batch job is a gap with a specific, closeable window — find out
  if that window exists before an inspector does.
- **Distinguish temporary from permanent deferrals when you review any exception request.** A
  hemoglobin deferral under 630.10(f)(3) is temporary — Marcus can be retested and cleared later.
  A deferral tied to evidence of a relevant transfusion-transmitted infection under 630.10(e)(1)
  is a different category entirely, often indefinite. If someone proposes a system workaround
  ("just let him try again next week"), the first question is which kind of deferral you're
  looking at.
- **Treat every eligibility determination as a decision that has to be traceable to a person and
  a basis, not a step that was completed.** "Cleared" isn't enough in a donor record; who
  determined it, and on what specific criteria, has to be reconstructable the way 630.10(d)
  through (g) require.
- **When a registration or BECS change is proposed, ask how it validates identity against the
  deferral registry before it touches anything else.** That single check is the control this
  entire module is built around — everything else in the pipeline assumes it already ran
  correctly.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Thursday's registration clerk says, "I don't need to check the deferral registry — he told me he wasn't deferred anywhere." Is a donor's own statement enough under 630.10?

No. 630.10(d)(1) requires the establishment to *consult the records of deferred donors* before
collection — an affirmative check, not a question the donor answers. 630.10(g)(1) separately
requires proof of identity, not a self-reported name. Both requirements exist specifically
because donor self-report isn't a substitute for either: a donor might not remember, might not
realize a hemoglobin deferral counts, or — rarely — might not be telling the truth. The registry
check has to run regardless of what the donor says.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Is the specific wording of the Donor History Questionnaire — the actual list of questions asked — itself set word-for-word by 21 CFR 630.10?

Not quite. 630.10(e) requires the establishment to *assess* a defined list of risk-factor
categories (behaviors and exposures associated with transfusion-transmitted infection, recent
illness, certain medications, travel, pregnancy, and others named in the section) — but the
regulation doesn't script the exact questions a donor answers. The standardized questionnaire
donors actually fill out across most U.S. blood centers is an industry-developed instrument,
built to satisfy 630.10(e)'s required categories, not text codified in the CFR itself. That
distinction matters the way it did in the regulatory-landscape foundation lesson: the
*requirement to assess* is regulation; the *specific script* used to do it is industry practice
built on top of the regulation, not the regulation's own verbatim text.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Marcus's hemoglobin deferral on Monday — does that mean he's permanently barred from donating at Lakeshore?

No. A hemoglobin or hematocrit deferral under 630.10(f)(3) is a temporary, retestable condition
— Marcus can come back once his levels are in range and go through eligibility screening again
like any other donor. That's different from a deferral tied to a relevant
transfusion-transmitted infection risk factor under 630.10(e)(1), which can be indefinite or
permanent depending on the specific factor involved. 630.40(b)(2) reflects this directly: part
of what Lakeshore's notification to a deferred donor must cover is, "where appropriate, the
types of donation... that the donor should not donate in the future" — meaning the notification
itself is expected to say whether this is temporary or something more permanent. Treating every
deferral as identical is a mistake in both directions: it either turns a same-week retest into a
lifetime ban, or it treats a serious, indefinite deferral as a minor speed bump.
:::

## Where this goes next

Marcus has either been correctly stopped or correctly cleared — either way, the eligibility
decision has been made and documented, and a donor who's eligible has consented to donate. That's
where this module ends. Module 2, `collection-and-testing`, picks up at the needle: the donation
event itself, the donor-to-unit identity link, and the infectious-disease and blood-typing panel
that has to clear before any of this ever becomes a product a hospital can use.
